$comment: Content for Justice League: Rights Edition (node g35, ages 15-18, Chapter 5), NEW v2 build to GDD 35
(mechanic-embodying), the rights-&-redress node (Thread G · Values, Rights & Media). "You have rights, there
are laws that protect you, and there are real ways to get help and justice: knowing them is your superpower."
84 researched, India-grounded scenarios across know-your-rights → know-the-law → get-justice → rights-in-action
→ educational-not-advice → your-rights-toolkit, each encoded as one of the shared v2 play actions (branch /
reflect / sort / match / strike-rewrite / spot / role-play): no binary "tap the right card". Lead: branch
(your move), match (law->plain meaning), strike-rewrite (bust the myth). Empowerment through knowledge: a
person who knows their rights and how to claim them is far harder to exploit and better able to help others.
EDUCATIONAL, NOT legal advice: translates law into plain language, demystifies redress, points to real
authorities and free legal aid; never promises outcomes. India framework: constitutional rights (equality,
dignity, RTE), POCSO (age of consent 18), POSH Act (workplace IC), Prohibition of Child Marriage Act (18/21),
DV Act, cyber-law; routes a trusted adult, police/FIR (Zero FIR, any station), school/college Internal
Committees, Child Welfare Committees, NCPCR/women's commissions, free legal aid via NALSA (15100, Article 39A),
and helplines (Childline 1098, Women 181, women-in-distress 1091, emergency 112, cybercrime 1930). Live danger
routes to help. Builds on g20 (Defenders); pairs g34 (Change Makers); underwrites g31 (Mutual). gameId
title: Justice League: Rights
greet: Hey, I’m Lensy. ⚖️ You have rights, laws protect you, and there are real ways to get justice. Knowing them makes you harder to exploit. (Learning, not advice.)

badge.title: Justice League: Rights ⚖️
badge.blurb: You know your rights, can read the law in plain language, and know the real paths to help and justice. That's your superpower against exploitation. 💪

helpLine: Tell a trusted adult; free legal aid NALSA 15100; Childline 1098, Women 181, women-in-distress 1091, emergency 112, cybercrime 1930.
reassure: Knowing your rights is power, and you’re never alone. Real routes: a trusted adult, free legal aid NALSA 15100, helplines 1098, 181, 1091, 112, 1930. ⚖️

scenarios.hook: "Rights are for adults and powerful people, not someone like me."

myth.un: Rights are for adults and the powerful, not me.
myth.re: Every person, including every teen, holds rights, they aren't a favour for the lucky few.
myth.why: Rights are guaranteed by the Constitution and law for all.

scenarios.relearn: Rights belong to everyone, including you; they're not just for the powerful.

scenarios.hook: "You have to earn your rights by behaving."

myth.un: You have to earn your rights.
myth.re: Rights aren't earned or granted as a reward; you have them simply as a person.
myth.why: They're guaranteed, not conditional on approval.

scenarios.relearn: Rights aren't earned; you hold them simply by being a person.

scenarios.hook: Match the right to what it means for you.

scenarios.hook: A boy from another school keeps threatening you over a fight you weren't even part of.

steps.prompt: You don't know what the first move should be. What do you do?

options.text: Gather your friends to face him after school
options.then: Your friends are up for it, and a bigger fight starts to look likely.

options.text: Believe you must sort it out alone to look strong
options.then: You carry it by yourself, and the messages keep coming.

options.text: Tell a trusted adult, like a teacher or counsellor
options.then: Mr Iyer listens, notes the details and says he'll help you plan.

options.text: Ask an older cousin to 'have a word' with him
options.then: Your cousin talks about bringing his friends along, which worries you.

steps.why: A trusted adult means you're not handling it alone. That's the first step to real help.

steps.prompt: The boy messages that he'll be waiting at your bus stop. What do you do?

options.text: Reply with a threat of your own
options.then: He replies with something worse, and things heat up.

options.text: Go to the bus stop to face him and end it
options.then: You see he's brought friends, and you turn back.

options.text: Show an adult and plan a safe way home
options.then: Your father picks you up and keeps a copy of the message.

options.text: Ask a friend whether it's a real threat
options.then: Your friend says he's 'probably bluffing', which doesn't get you home.

steps.why: Planning with an adult keeps you safe now, and the saved message is proof.

steps.prompt: A week later, the threats still haven't stopped. What do you do?

options.text: Believe it's your fault for having those friends
options.then: You pull away from your friends, and the threats carry on.

options.text: Post his messages online to shame him
options.then: His friends pile into your comments, and it spreads.

options.text: Report it with an adult, bringing the messages
options.then: Your father and the counsellor contact his school, with the messages as proof.

options.text: Set up a 'final fight' to settle it
options.then: Word spreads, and teachers hear a fight is being planned.

steps.why: Real routes, with an adult beside you, can stop threats a fight can't. It's never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: The first route to justice is almost always a trusted adult.
scenarios.relearn: First step to justice: tell a trusted adult, teacher or counsellor.

scenarios.hook: "The police can just refuse to register your complaint."

myth.un: The police can refuse to register your complaint.
myth.re: For a serious (cognizable) offence, registering an FIR is mandatory; and a Zero FIR can be filed at any police station.
myth.why: The Supreme Court made FIR registration mandatory for such offences.

scenarios.relearn: For a serious offence, an FIR is mandatory, and a Zero FIR can be filed anywhere.

scenarios.relearn: FIRs, Internal Committees and free legal aid are real routes to justice.

scenarios.hook: "You can't get justice without money for a lawyer."

myth.un: You can't get justice without money for a lawyer.
myth.re: Free legal aid is available to those who can't afford one, through the Legal Services Authorities.
myth.why: Justice can't be denied for lack of money (Article 39A).

scenarios.relearn: Free legal aid exists for those who can't afford a lawyer (NALSA, 15100).

scenarios.hook: At your weekend job in a clothes store, a co-worker keeps making sexual comments about you.

steps.prompt: You've started dreading every shift. What do you do?

options.text: Believe this is just how jobs work
options.then: The comments carry on, and each shift feels longer.

options.text: Tell a trusted adult, and ask how to complain
options.then: Your mother listens and says, 'This isn't okay. Let's find out who handles it.'

options.text: Wonder if your clothes give him the wrong idea
options.then: You start changing what you wear, and he doesn't change at all.

options.text: Take a co-worker's advice to just ignore him
options.then: She shrugs that he's like that with everyone, and nothing changes.

steps.why: Telling a trusted adult means you don't face it alone. It's never your fault.

steps.prompt: You learn that workplaces should have an Internal Committee for harassment. What do you do?

options.text: Decide part-timers probably can't use it
options.then: You never check, and the route stays out of reach.

options.text: Find out who's on it, with an adult's help
options.then: Your aunt helps you find the committee's contact on the staff notice board.

options.text: Complain to the co-worker's friends instead
options.then: They tell him, and he smirks at you the next shift.

options.text: Believe a complaint would cost you the job
options.then: You never ask, and the committee stays unused, though using it is your right.

steps.why: The committee is there for every worker, part-time too. Using it is your right.

steps.prompt: A week later, he tells everyone you 'can't take a joke'. What do you do?

options.text: Wonder if you really can't take a joke
options.then: You doubt yourself all evening, and nothing has changed by your next shift.

options.text: Snap back with an insult in front of everyone
options.then: The manager only sees your outburst and asks you to calm down.

options.text: Ask a colleague to tell him off for you
options.then: She has a word with him, and he jokes about it the next day.

options.text: Note what happened, with dates, for the committee
options.then: Your notes are clear, and your aunt helps you send them in.

steps.why: Dated notes make a complaint clear, and it helps to use the route soon.

steps.prompt: Your manager says the store doesn't need 'drama' and asks you to keep things friendly. What do you do?

options.text: Believe the manager's word overrides the committee
options.then: You wait for him to fix it, and he never does.

options.text: Post about the store and the manager online
options.then: The post spreads, and the store asks your family to have it taken down.

options.text: Use the committee anyway, with an adult's support
options.then: Your mother says she'll come with you to meet the committee.

options.text: Ask a friend's father to threaten the co-worker
options.then: He confronts the co-worker at the store, and it turns into a shouting match.

steps.why: Pressure to stay quiet doesn't cancel your right to complain. An adult beside you helps.

scenarios.debrief: Workplace harassment has a committee route for complaints. Using it is your right, and it's never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: For workplace harassment, use the Internal Committee and tell an adult.

scenarios.relearn: Childline 1098, Women 181 and Cybercrime 1930 connect to immediate help.

scenarios.hook: On the way home, a group of men surround your friend Rahul and start shoving him.

steps.prompt: Nobody nearby has stepped in yet. What do you do?

options.text: Look up which law covers this first
options.then: The page is still loading, and the shoving gets rougher.

options.text: Jump in and fight them yourself
options.then: One of them turns on you, and now you're both in danger.

options.text: Film it to post later as proof
options.then: You get the video, but nobody has called for help.

options.text: Call 112 and shout for nearby adults
options.then: A shopkeeper rushes out, and the operator says a patrol is coming.

steps.why: In immediate danger, call 112 and get adults. The law can wait.

steps.prompt: The men run off, and Rahul is shaken with a cut on his arm. What do you do next?

options.text: Stay with him and call his parents
options.then: His mother arrives fast and takes him to get the cut seen to.

options.text: Tell him to clean up and go home
options.then: He agrees, but no adult knows what happened.

options.text: Post about it to track the men down
options.then: Comments fill with guesses and threats, and Rahul is upset.

options.text: Get him to help you chase after them
options.then: Rahul is too shaken to move and says he wants to go home.

steps.why: After danger, a trusted adult helps with care and next steps. It's never Rahul's fault.

steps.prompt: Next day, Rahul wonders if it's worth reporting, since he's okay now. What do you say?

options.text: That it's pointless, since nobody was badly hurt
options.then: He drops it, wondering if the men will try it again.

options.text: That he can report it, and you'll go with him
options.then: He nods slowly and says he'll ask his parents to come too.

options.text: That the two of you can find them yourselves
options.then: Rahul shakes his head. He doesn't want another fight.

options.text: That he'll definitely get them all arrested
options.then: He feels hopeful, then confused when the officer says it takes time.

steps.why: Reporting with support is a real route, even though no one can promise an outcome.

scenarios.debrief: Immediate danger means emergency help first. The law comes after.
scenarios.relearn: In immediate danger, call 112 and get a trusted adult first.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Meher says a man from her coaching centre keeps following her home.
scenarios.setup: She's crying in the school washroom.

steps.prompt: Meher asks: "If I tell anyone, won't it just make things worse?"

options.text: "You can report this. I'll come with you to a teacher."
options.then: Meher wipes her eyes. "You'd really come? Okay."

options.text: "You'll probably just get into trouble for telling."
options.then: Meher's face drops. "So I just put up with it?"

options.text: "Just take a different road home for now."
options.then: She nods, then whispers, "He knows the other road too."

options.text: "I'll get my brother to go and scare him off."
options.then: Meher panics. "No! That'll only make him angrier."

steps.why: Naming her right and offering to go with her makes the first step feel possible.

steps.prompt: The next morning, Meher says: "If I tell a teacher, what if she doesn't believe me?"

options.text: "Teachers always believe girls. Don't worry about it."
options.then: Meher frowns. "Not always. You can't know that."

options.text: "Then we try the counsellor. We don't stop at one no."
options.then: Meher manages a small smile. "Okay. Two tries, at least."

options.text: "Maybe wait until you have more proof."
options.then: Meher agrees to wait. "He was outside again last night," she adds.

options.text: "I'll do all the talking. You can just stand there."
options.then: Meher hesitates. "But it's my thing to say."

steps.why: Planning a backup keeps her going without promising what no one can guarantee.

steps.prompt: Later, Meher asks quietly: "Do you think this is somehow my fault?"

options.text: "Maybe stop wearing the earrings he commented on."
options.then: Meher touches her ears and goes quiet.

options.text: "Don't think about fault. Just try to forget him."
options.then: "I can't just forget," Meher says, hugging her bag.

options.text: "No. It's his behaviour, not anything you did."
options.then: Meher breathes out. "I needed someone to say that."

options.text: "Everyone gets followed sometimes. It's normal."
options.then: "It doesn't feel normal," Meher says, very quietly.

steps.why: It is never her fault. Saying so plainly helps her keep going.

scenarios.relearn: Remind a scared friend they have the right to report, and go with them.

scenarios.hook: Someone keeps posting edited photos of you in the class group.
scenarios.setup: You stop Ms. Fernandes after class.

steps.prompt: Ms. Fernandes asks: "Yes? Is something wrong?"

options.text: "It's probably nothing. I'm just being sensitive."
options.then: She hesitates. "Are you sure? You look upset."

options.text: "Can you tell the whole class off for me?"
options.then: "For what, exactly?" she asks, puzzled.

options.text: "Something happened, and I need help reporting it."
options.then: She puts her bag down. "Of course. Tell me what's going on."

options.text: "Some people are being really mean, ma'am."
options.then: She pauses. "Mean how? Tell me a bit more."

steps.why: A clear ask tells her to stop and listen. What's being done to you is not your fault.

steps.prompt: Ms. Fernandes says: "I want to help. What exactly is happening?"

options.text: "Maybe it's only jokes, and I'm overreacting."
options.then: She frowns. "If it upset you, you're not overreacting."

options.text: "Edited photos of me are being posted. I saved them."
options.then: She nods. "Show me. We'll take this to the counsellor today."

options.text: "It's online, so school can't do anything, right?"
options.then: She shakes her head. "Online or not, it's our class. Tell me."

options.text: "I'll deal with them myself. I just wanted you to know."
options.then: "Please don't," she says. "Let's handle it properly."

steps.why: Plain facts and saved proof give her what she needs to act.

steps.prompt: The next day, Ms. Fernandes says: "I asked around and saw the photos. I'm taking this further."

options.text: "Can you promise they'll be suspended?"
options.then: "I can't promise outcomes," she says gently. "I can promise to act."

options.text: "Can we just get the photos deleted and drop it?"
options.then: "Deleting them is part of it," she says, "but this needs more than that."

options.text: "Can you tell me what happens next, so I know?"
options.then: "Of course. First the counsellor, then we speak to the group's admins."

options.text: "Can I post in the group that I've reported it?"
options.then: She shakes her head. "That could stir things up. Leave it with us."

steps.why: Knowing the next steps keeps you part of the process without demanding an outcome.

scenarios.relearn: A clear ask to a trusted adult starts the route to help.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a real route to justice, or not?

items.text: Filing an FIR with the police

scenarios.relearn: FIRs and free legal aid are real routes; revenge and angry posts aren't.

scenarios.hook: Pinky, 8, from next door often has bruises, and you hear her crying late at night.

steps.prompt: Your parents say it's her family's business. What do you do?

options.text: Agree it's their business and stay out of it
options.then: The crying carries on, on other nights.

options.text: Confront Pinky's father yourself
options.then: He slams the door and tells your parents you were rude.

options.text: Call Childline 1098 for advice
options.then: The person on the line listens and asks for the area, so they can check on her.

options.text: Ask Pinky directly who is hurting her
options.then: Pinky looks frightened and runs inside.

steps.why: A child at risk is never private business. Childline 1098 is built for exactly this.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Pinky quietly tells you her father hits her when he's angry. What do you do?

options.text: Ask her exactly what he does, and how often
options.then: Pinky gets scared by the questions and goes quiet.

options.text: Promise her you won't tell anyone at all, ever
options.then: She smiles a little, and you're left with a secret too big to keep.

options.text: Say you're glad she told you. It's not her fault
options.then: Pinky nods slowly and holds your hand for a moment.

options.text: Tell her to be extra good so he stays calm
options.then: Pinky nods seriously, as if it's her job to fix it.

steps.why: Believing her calmly, without questions, helps her feel safe. It's never a child's fault.

steps.prompt: That evening, you want to be sure someone acts. What do you do?

options.text: Post about the neighbours in the colony group
options.then: The group erupts, and Pinky's family is furious with her.

options.text: Wait to see if things get better on their own
options.then: Another week passes, and you hear her crying again.

options.text: Tell your parents, and call 1098 together
options.then: Your mother listens, then sits with you while you call.

options.text: Go and warn Pinky's father yourself
options.then: He shouts at you to leave, and you worry about Pinky afterwards.

steps.why: Childline and a trusted adult can act for Pinky in ways you can't alone.

steps.prompt: Later, a neighbour says calling Childline will 'break up the family'. What do you say?

options.text: That you'll back off if it causes trouble
options.then: The neighbour nods, and Pinky is left without help.

options.text: That her parents deserve to be in jail
options.then: The neighbour turns away, and the colony starts taking sides.

options.text: That she'll surely be taken away from them
options.then: The neighbour gets alarmed and warns Pinky's parents.

options.text: That Childline is there to keep Pinky safe
options.then: The neighbour pauses, then says she is only small.

steps.why: Child protection is about keeping the child safe, not punishing a family.

scenarios.debrief: Child protection has dedicated routes. A child's safety isn't 'private business'.
scenarios.relearn: For a child at risk: Childline 1098, a Child Welfare Committee, or a trusted adult.

scenarios.hook: Match the step to where it comes in the path.

pairs.left: If you can't afford a lawyer

scenarios.relearn: The path: trusted adult, then FIR if needed, with free legal aid available.

scenarios.hook: A man on a bike snatched your phone and knocked you over on your way home.

steps.prompt: You worry the police will brush off a teenager. What do you do?

options.text: Believe a teenager's complaint won't count
options.then: You stay home, and the phone and its photos feel gone for good.

options.text: Report it with a parent, knowing your rights
options.then: Your father comes along, and you both walk in calm and prepared.

options.text: Track the phone and go get it back yourself
options.then: The map shows a crowded market, and going alone feels risky.

options.text: Post about it and hope someone finds the man
options.then: People share it, but nobody who can act gets involved.

steps.why: Knowing serious crimes must be registered, and bringing an adult, means you go in informed.

steps.prompt: A neighbour warns that snatchings sometimes get written down as 'lost phones'. What do you do?

options.text: Plan to accept 'lost' if offered, to keep it simple
options.then: It would be quicker, but the snatching would never be on record.

options.text: Bring an uncle who says he has 'contacts'
options.then: Your uncle talks about calling someone important, which makes you uneasy.

options.text: Plan to say it was snatched, and ask for an FIR
options.then: You write down exactly what happened, with the time and place.

options.text: Plan to argue loudly until they give in
options.then: You picture a shouting match, which could make things harder.

steps.why: Describing it as it happened, and asking for an FIR, is your right for a serious crime.

steps.prompt: When you report it, the officer seems reluctant to write it down. What do you do?

options.text: Offer some money to 'speed things up'
options.then: The officer frowns, and things get more complicated.

options.text: Calmly ask for an FIR for a serious crime
options.then: The officer pauses, then starts the paperwork.

options.text: Say you'll post a video of him online
options.then: He gets defensive, and the room turns tense.

options.text: Accept a 'lost phone' note just to get it done
options.then: You leave with a paper that doesn't mention the snatching.

steps.why: For a serious crime, registering an FIR isn't optional. Asking calmly is your right.

scenarios.debrief: Knowing the rules and bringing support makes being turned away far less likely. Being robbed is never your fault.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Kabir was beaten up and robbed by older boys near the bus stand.
scenarios.setup: He tells you on the walk to school.

steps.prompt: Kabir says: "Don't tell anyone. They said they'd come back."

options.text: "Okay. I won't say a word to anyone, ever."
options.then: Kabir relaxes. "Thanks. Let's just forget it."

options.text: "You have every right to report this. I'll come with you."
options.then: Kabir hesitates. "You'd come? What if they see us?"

options.text: "You'll probably just get into trouble, so leave it."
options.then: Kabir nods grimly. "That's what I thought."

options.text: "Let's find them after school and get your stuff back."
options.then: Kabir goes pale. "Are you mad? There were four of them."

steps.why: Naming his right and offering to go along beats keeping a risky secret.

steps.prompt: At lunch, Kabir says: "I keep thinking they'll come back. Who could we even tell?"

options.text: "Mr. Rao. He listens, and he'll know what to do."
options.then: Kabir thinks. "He did help Sunil last year."

options.text: "Your dad. He'll go straight there and beat them."
options.then: "That's exactly what I'm scared of," Kabir says.

options.text: "Their parents, so they get a proper scolding."
options.then: "We don't even know who their parents are," he says.

options.text: "No one yet. Let's wait and see if they come back."
options.then: Kabir nods, but keeps glancing at the gate.

steps.why: A trusted teacher can get real help moving without making things riskier.

steps.prompt: Kabir asks: "Will the police even care about a stolen phone?"

options.text: "Probably not. Phones get stolen every day."
options.then: Kabir shrugs. "So what's the point?"

options.text: "They'll catch them for sure. Don't worry."
options.then: "For sure?" Kabir says. "You can't know that."

options.text: "They hurt you and robbed you. That's serious."
options.then: Kabir looks up. "I guess it is, when you say it like that."

options.text: "Forget the phone. Just be glad you're okay."
options.then: "It's not just the phone," he mutters. "They hit me."

steps.why: Robbery with violence is serious, and a trusted adult can help him report it properly.

steps.prompt: Before class, Kabir says: "I feel like such a coward for not fighting back."

options.text: "Next time, just hit back harder."
options.then: Kabir clenches his jaw. "Maybe I should have."

options.text: "Honestly, you should've just run for it."
options.then: Kabir's face falls. "I tried."

options.text: "Don't think about it. Let's talk about something else."
options.then: He goes quiet, still turning it over.

options.text: "You did what kept you safe. None of this is your fault."
options.then: Kabir looks up. "Yeah. Okay. Let's do this."

steps.why: Not fighting back is how people stay safe. It is never his fault.

scenarios.relearn: Remind a scared friend they have the right to report, and go with them.

scenarios.hook: Some seniors keep shoving you and calling you names in the corridor.
scenarios.setup: You find Mr. Sharma alone in the lab.

steps.prompt: Mr. Sharma asks: "You look tense. Need something?"

options.text: "Do people ever get in trouble for complaining?"
options.then: "Why do you ask?" he says, a little puzzled.

options.text: "Yes, sir. I need help making a complaint."
options.then: He sets down the beaker. "Of course. Sit. What happened?"

options.text: "Is it my fault if people don't like me?"
options.then: He frowns. "What makes you say that?"

options.text: "Can you make some seniors leave me alone?"
options.then: "Which seniors? What are they doing?" he asks.

steps.why: Saying plainly that you want to complain tells him to help. None of this is your fault.

steps.prompt: Mr. Sharma says: "Tell me what's been happening, from the start."

options.text: "They're just bullies. Everyone in school knows that."
options.then: "I'll need more than that," he says gently.

options.text: "It's not that bad. Maybe I'm overreacting."
options.then: "If it's bothering you, it matters," he says. "Tell me more."

options.text: "Three seniors shove me daily. I've noted the dates."
options.then: He nods, writing. "Dates help a lot. Go on."

options.text: "Can you just suspend them today, sir?"
options.then: "I can't do that alone," he says. "First, tell me what happened."

steps.why: Clear facts and dates give him what he needs to act.

steps.prompt: The next day, Mr. Sharma says: "I saw it myself today. I'm taking it to the discipline committee."

options.text: "Only if you promise they'll be expelled."
options.then: "I can't promise that," he says. "I can promise it's taken seriously."

options.text: "Yes. What happens after that?"
options.then: "They'll meet you first, with me there," he says.

options.text: "Can't you just warn them quietly instead?"
options.then: "A quiet warning may not stop it," he says, frowning.

options.text: "Should I tell them myself that I've complained?"
options.then: "Please don't," he says quickly. "Let us handle that."

steps.why: Agreeing to the proper route, and asking what comes next, keeps you informed and safe.

scenarios.relearn: A clear ask to a trusted adult starts the route to help.

scenarios.setup: She brings it up in the canteen.

steps.prompt: Divya says: "A lawyer would cost more than we even lost."

options.text: "Yeah, money decides everything, so maybe let it go."

options.text: "Cost isn't the wall. Call 15100 for free legal aid."
options.then: Divya blinks. "Free? Even for something like this?"

options.text: "Start a crowdfunding page to pay for a lawyer."
options.then: "Who'd give money for that?" she says doubtfully.

options.text: "Get a reporter to shame the builder publicly."
options.then: "And then he sues us," she says, alarmed.

steps.prompt: The next day, Divya says: "I read about free legal aid. Isn't it only for really poor people?"

options.text: "Anyone can get it, with no questions asked at all."
options.then: "Really? No conditions at all?" She sounds unsure.

options.text: "It's for people who can't afford a lawyer. Ask them."
options.then: She nods slowly. "Asking costs nothing, I guess."

options.text: "Probably. You don't look poor enough to get it."
options.then: Divya laughs awkwardly. "So that's a no?"

options.text: "I'm not sure. Let's just forget it."
options.then: She shrugs. "Okay. Back to square one."

options.text: "You won't lose. The builder's clearly guilty."
options.then: "You can't know that," she says, but looks hopeful anyway.

options.text: "Then why bother at all?"

options.text: "Let your parents deal with it. It's not your problem."
options.then: "They don't know about free aid either," she says.

options.text: "Maybe. But a lawyer can tell you your real options."
options.then: "Real options," she repeats. "That's more than we have now."

steps.why: No one can promise a win, but qualified help shows the real options.

scenarios.hook: You were robbed at knifepoint, and your uncle takes you to the police station.
scenarios.setup: The officer at the desk barely looks up.

steps.prompt: The officer says: "Phones get stolen daily. Come back if it turns up."

options.text: "Please, sir. Just write it down somewhere."
options.then: He scribbles a line in a register. "Done. You can go."

options.text: "I was threatened with a knife. I'd like to file an FIR."
options.then: He looks up properly for the first time. "A knife? Sit down."

options.text: "My uncle knows someone senior. Should we call him?"
options.then: The officer's face hardens. "Call whoever you like."

options.text: "Is it even a crime if the phone was a cheap one?"
options.then: "Exactly. Not worth the paperwork," he says.

steps.why: Naming the serious offence and asking for an FIR keeps it on the facts. The robbery is not your fault.

steps.prompt: Your uncle asks about an FIR. The officer says: "That takes hours. Why not just a written complaint?"

options.text: "A written complaint will do for now, I suppose."
options.then: "Good," he says, filing the page away. "We'll call you."

options.text: "I'll post online that you refused to help us."
options.then: His jaw tightens. "Go ahead. Next."

options.text: "For a serious offence, I understand an FIR is mandatory."
options.then: He pauses, then pulls out a form. "Name and address?"

options.text: "Can we pay something extra to speed it all up?"
options.then: "Careful what you're suggesting," he says coldly.

steps.why: For a serious offence an FIR is mandatory, and saying so calmly is your right.

steps.prompt: A senior officer stops at the desk and asks: "What brings you here?"

options.text: "This officer has been useless and rude to us, ma'am."
options.then: Her eyes narrow. "Let's keep this civil."

options.text: "Can you just get my phone back, please?"
options.then: "That needs a case first," she says. "Has one been filed?"

options.text: "My uncle will explain it. I'm too young to really know."
options.then: She turns to you. "You were there. I'd like to hear it from you."

options.text: "I was robbed at knifepoint. I'm here to file an FIR."
options.then: She nods to the desk. "Let's hear it properly, then."

steps.why: Stating plainly what happened and why you're there keeps it on the facts, even with a senior officer.

scenarios.relearn: For a serious offence you can calmly state that an FIR is mandatory.

scenarios.hook: Varun says the law on child sexual abuse only protects girls.
scenarios.setup: Others at the canteen table nod along.

steps.prompt: Varun says: "Boys can't be victims. Everyone knows that."

options.text: "You're probably right. It's a girls' thing."
options.then: Varun grins. "See? Even you agree."

options.text: "Only someone clueless would say that, Varun."
options.then: Varun bristles. "Whatever. Prove it, then."

options.text: "It protects every child under 18, boys too."
options.then: Varun frowns. "Really? I always heard it was for girls."

options.text: "Maybe it's changed. I'm not totally sure."
options.then: Varun shrugs. "Then don't act like an expert."

steps.why: The law protects every child under 18, of any gender.

steps.prompt: Later, Varun asks: "Seriously, though. Could a boy who was abused report it?"

options.text: "Technically, but people would laugh at him."
options.then: "Exactly why no one does," Varun says.

options.text: "Yes. A trusted adult or Childline 1098 can help."
options.then: Varun nods slowly. "I didn't know that."

options.text: "Only if he has proof and a witness."
options.then: "So basically never," Varun says.

options.text: "He'd honestly be better off forgetting it."
options.then: Varun shrugs. "Yeah, that's what I'd do."

steps.why: Any child can reach help through a trusted adult or Childline 1098.

steps.prompt: Later, Varun says quietly: "Wouldn't a boy be too ashamed to tell anyone?"

options.text: "Yeah. Real men handle things on their own."
options.then: Varun nods, but looks away.

options.text: "Only if he somehow let it happen to him."
options.then: Varun winces. "That's harsh."

options.text: "Maybe. But it's never his fault, and help is there."
options.then: Varun is quiet for a while. "I'll remember that."

options.text: "Let's not talk about this stuff. It's too awkward."
options.then: Varun shrugs and changes the subject.

steps.why: Shame keeps boys silent. Knowing it's never their fault helps them reach help.

scenarios.relearn: The law on child sexual abuse protects every child under 18, whatever their gender.

scenarios.hook: At a family function, your uncle says cousin Pooja, 16, will be married soon.
scenarios.setup: Someone asks if that isn't too young.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "That's the family's business, no one else's."

options.text: "I guess if the family decided, nobody can say anything."
options.then: Your uncle nods. "Exactly. Now eat."

options.text: "Under 18, it's not just family business. It's the law."
options.then: Your uncle frowns. "What law? We're doing nothing wrong."

options.text: "That's disgusting. You should be ashamed of it."
options.then: The room goes quiet. Your uncle stands up stiffly.

options.text: "Shouldn't someone at least ask Pooja what she wants?"
options.then: "She's happy," he says. "Ask her yourself."

steps.why: Calmly naming the law moves it from family opinion to a legal fact.

steps.prompt: When someone else objects, your uncle says: "Pooja agreed. Isn't that enough?"

options.text: "Oh. If she agreed, then I suppose it's fine."
options.then: He nods, satisfied. "Exactly."

options.text: "Even if she agrees, the minimum age for women is 18."
options.then: He pauses. "Since when does the law decide that?"

options.text: "She only agreed because you all pressured her into it."
options.then: His face darkens. "Watch your tone."

options.text: "Let's ask her right now, in front of everyone."
options.then: Pooja looks mortified as everyone turns to her.

steps.why: The minimum marriage age is 18 for women and 21 for men, whoever agrees.

steps.prompt: Later, your aunt pulls you aside and says: "Don't make trouble for the family."

options.text: "Fine. I'll stay out of it from now on, then."
options.then: "Good," she says, relieved, and hurries back.

options.text: "The whole family should be reported for this, honestly."
options.then: She steps back, hurt. "We're your family."

options.text: "I care about Pooja. I'll talk to a teacher and Childline 1098."
options.then: Your aunt sighs. "I just want everyone safe and happy."

options.text: "Then I'll just talk Pooja into running away."
options.then: Your aunt goes pale. "Don't you dare."

steps.why: A teacher and Childline 1098 can protect Pooja. That's care, and the pressure is never her fault.

scenarios.relearn: Marrying under the legal age is a legal matter: 18 for women and 21 for men.

scenarios.hook: Your internship boss keeps commenting on your looks in meetings.
scenarios.setup: Over chai, a senior intern notices you're upset.

steps.prompt: The senior intern says: "That's normal here. Just ignore it."

options.text: "Maybe I'm just too sensitive about it."
options.then: She shrugs. "Everyone gets used to it."

options.text: "It's not normal. I'll tell my mum and the Internal Committee."
options.then: She looks surprised. "There's a committee? I never knew."

options.text: "I'll tell him off in front of everyone tomorrow."
options.then: Her eyes widen. "In the meeting? That could get ugly."

options.text: "Interns can't complain anyway. We're not real staff."
options.then: She nods. "That's what I always thought too."

steps.why: Interns are covered too. The Internal Committee is the route, a trusted adult helps, and it's never your fault.

steps.prompt: She adds: "Even if you complained, wouldn't they take his side? He's the boss."

options.text: "Probably. Bosses always win these things."
options.then: She nods. "That's why I never said anything."

options.text: "Not if I get everyone to sign a petition first."
options.then: "People won't sign against the boss," she says.

options.text: "I'll record him secretly and post it online."
options.then: She looks worried. "That could backfire on you."

options.text: "The committee has to hear it fairly. That's its job."
options.then: "Huh," she says. "Then maybe it's worth trying."

steps.why: The committee is set up to hear complaints fairly, even about a boss.

steps.prompt: She says: "If you complain, I'll back you up. I've heard him too."

options.text: "Thank you. Would you write down what you heard?"
options.then: She nods. "I'll do it tonight."

options.text: "Great. Then can you file it for me?"
options.then: She hesitates. "It's your complaint, though."

options.text: "Let's get the other interns and confront him."
options.then: She shakes her head. "That'll turn into a mess."

options.text: "No, I don't want you dragged into it."
options.then: She shrugs. "Okay. The offer stands."

steps.why: A witness's written account makes a complaint stronger.

scenarios.relearn: Workplace harassment has a route: the Internal Committee.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Zoya gets abusive messages every night from a fake account.
scenarios.setup: She shows you her phone at the bus stop.

steps.prompt: Zoya says: "It's just the internet. Nothing can be done."

options.text: "Yeah. Just block it and forget about it."
options.then: Zoya sighs. "I've blocked four already. They keep coming back."

options.text: "Reply and tell them off properly."
options.then: Zoya hesitates. "Won't that just make them worse?"

options.text: "It's a real crime. You can report it at 1930."
options.then: Zoya looks up. "A real crime? I thought it was just trolling."

options.text: "Maybe stay off your phone for a while."
options.then: Zoya's face falls. "Why should I be the one to hide?"

steps.why: Online abuse is covered by law and can be reported. It's never Zoya's fault.

steps.prompt: The next day, Zoya says: "My cousin says I should report it. What would I need?"

options.text: "Nothing. Just tell them roughly what happened."
options.then: "Without any proof?" she says doubtfully.

options.text: "Screenshots with dates and the account name."
options.then: She starts screenshotting. "Okay. I have a lot."

options.text: "Find out who it is first, then report them."
options.then: "How would I even find out?" she asks.

options.text: "Delete it all. Seeing it only hurts you."
options.then: She almost does, then stops. "But then there's no proof."

steps.why: Saved screenshots are the evidence a report needs.

steps.prompt: Zoya says: "My parents will freak out if they find out."

options.text: "Then just hide it and handle it on your own."
options.then: Zoya nods, but looks exhausted.

options.text: "Tell them with me there. They can help you report."
options.then: Zoya takes a breath. "Okay. Tonight, after dinner."

options.text: "Then I'll tell them for you today."
options.then: "No!" Zoya says. "Let me do it my way."

options.text: "Parents never understand this stuff anyway."
options.then: "True," she says, and the idea of help fades.

steps.why: A trusted adult can help her report, and going with her makes telling easier.

scenarios.relearn: Online abuse is a real crime; report it at cybercrime.gov.in / 1930.

scenarios.hook: Irfan's mother was let go without pay after getting hurt at the factory.
scenarios.setup: Irfan tells you on the bus home.

steps.prompt: Irfan says: "We can't afford a lawyer, so we can't do anything."

options.text: "Yeah, without money there's nothing you can do."
options.then: Irfan nods. "That's what Ammi keeps saying."

options.text: "Call 15100 for free legal aid. Cost needn't stop you."
options.then: Irfan pauses. "Free? You're sure it's real?"

options.text: "Ask the owner to pay her out of kindness, maybe."
options.then: "He won't even take her calls," Irfan says.

options.text: "Get everyone from your area to protest at the gate."
options.then: Irfan looks nervous. "Then no one will hire her again."

steps.why: Free legal aid on 15100 means cost shouldn't block justice.

steps.prompt: Later, Irfan says: "Someone told Ammi about free legal aid. Won't they look down on us?"

options.text: "Probably. Free stuff always comes with attitude."
options.then: "Then why bother?" he says.

options.text: "It exists for people who can't pay. It's your right."
options.then: Irfan nods. "A right. Not charity."

options.text: "Dress smart, so they take you seriously."
options.then: Irfan frowns. "So it's about clothes?"

options.text: "Skip it. Write to a news channel instead."
options.then: "They'd never cover us," he says.

steps.why: Free legal aid is a right, not a favour, for those who can't pay.

steps.prompt: Irfan says: "Ammi doesn't speak much English. Will that matter?"

options.text: "Yes. Legal stuff only happens in English."
options.then: Irfan's face falls. "Then it's hopeless."

options.text: "Let me call and pretend to be her."
options.then: "That's lying," Irfan says, uneasy.

options.text: "Sit with her when she calls, and help her explain."
options.then: Irfan smiles a little. "She'd like that."

options.text: "She should wait until her English is better."
options.then: Irfan laughs unhappily. "That would take years."

steps.why: Helping her make the call herself keeps it her case, with your support.

scenarios.relearn: Free legal aid (NALSA, 15100) means cost shouldn't block justice.

scenarios.hook: A man has been harassing your friend Simran on her walk home.
scenarios.setup: Simran is furious, phone in hand.

steps.prompt: Simran says: "I'm posting his photo and address everywhere tonight."

options.text: "Go for it. Expose him everywhere. He deserves it."
options.then: "Yes," Simran says, already typing. "Everyone should know."

options.text: "That could backfire on you. Let's report it properly."
options.then: Simran hesitates. "Backfire how? He's the one in the wrong."

options.text: "Post just his photo, and leave out the address."
options.then: "Fine," she says, cropping it. "It's still going up."

options.text: "Ignore him. Guys like that usually get bored."
options.then: "He's been at it for a month," she says flatly.

steps.why: Posting his details can put her at risk and hurt her case. Lawful routes protect her.

steps.prompt: A little later, Simran calms down and asks: "What would reporting even look like?"

options.text: "Just tell the security guard on your road."
options.then: "He's always asleep," Simran says.

options.text: "Get your brothers to go and deal with him."
options.then: "And then they're in trouble," she says.

options.text: "Save proof, tell your parents, and go to the police."
options.then: "With my parents," she repeats. "Okay. Less scary."

options.text: "Write an anonymous post in the area's group."
options.then: "Anonymous won't stop him," she says.

steps.why: Evidence, a trusted adult and the police make a route that actually protects her.

steps.prompt: Simran asks: "What if the police say it's not serious enough?"

options.text: "Then post it online after all."
options.then: "So it was all pointless," she mutters.

options.text: "They'll arrest him on the spot. Don't worry."
options.then: "On the spot?" She looks doubtful.

options.text: "Stalking is an offence. Your parents can insist."
options.then: Simran nods. "Then I'll keep a list of every time."

options.text: "Then just give up. At least you tried."
options.then: Simran looks at you. "That's it?"

steps.why: Stalking is a real offence, and a trusted adult can help insist on a report.

steps.prompt: Later, Simran asks: "If I stop walking that road, is that giving in?"

options.text: "Yes. Don't let him win. Keep walking it."
options.then: Simran frowns. "So I should just risk it?"

options.text: "You shouldn't go out alone at all now."
options.then: "At all?" she says. "That's not fair either."

options.text: "Well, you did choose that lonely road."
options.then: Simran stares at you, hurt.

options.text: "Staying safe isn't giving in. It's your call."
options.then: Simran nods slowly. "Maybe Papa can walk with me."

steps.why: Her safety choices are hers, and the harassment is never her fault.

scenarios.relearn: Save evidence and report the lawful way; doxxing can rebound on you.

scenarios.hook: Your 14-year-old brother Aarav thinks kids have no real protection until 18.

steps.prompt: Aarav says: "Laws are for adults. Kids just deal with stuff."

options.text: "Yeah, basically you're on your own till 18."
options.then: Aarav shrugs. "Figured."

options.text: "Not true. You're protected now, not only at 18."
options.then: Aarav looks up. "Wait, seriously? Like how?"

options.text: "Just listen to adults and you'll be fine."
options.then: "Even when they're wrong?" Aarav asks.

options.text: "Kids don't need laws. Parents protect them."
options.then: "What if it's not safe at home?" he asks.

steps.why: Children hold rights and protections right now, not only at 18.

steps.prompt: Aarav asks: "So who would a kid even call?"

options.text: "The police, but only if it's something really serious."
options.then: "How would I know what's serious?" he asks.

options.text: "Childline 1098, or a trusted adult like a teacher."
options.then: Aarav repeats it. "1098. Okay."

options.text: "Nobody. Better to sort things out yourself."
options.then: Aarav nods. "That's what I thought."

options.text: "Just google it when it happens."

scenarios.hook: Your family is choosing your college stream without asking you.
scenarios.setup: At dinner, you try to speak up.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "Kids don't get an opinion in this house."

options.text: "Maybe elders always know what's best for me."
options.then: Your uncle nods. "Exactly. Now eat."

options.text: "I'll listen, but I do get a say in my own future."
options.then: Your uncle raises an eyebrow. "Fine. What do you want, then?"

options.text: "This is so unfair. Nobody here ever listens!"
options.then: "See? This is why," your uncle says to the table.

options.text: "Fine. I'll just do what I want anyway."
options.then: "Then don't come to us later," he snaps.

steps.why: Calmly naming your say, while still listening, is how you claim it with respect.

steps.prompt: Your father asks: "So what is it you actually want to study?"

options.text: "I don't know yet. Just not engineering, please."
options.then: "That's not a plan," he says.

options.text: "Whatever. You'll all decide for me anyway."
options.then: He sighs. "Then why bring it up?"

options.text: "Design. I've looked at colleges. Can I show you?"
options.then: He leans back. "Okay. Show me."

options.text: "Something that pays better than your job."
options.then: His face tightens. "Is that so."

steps.why: A clear answer with a plan shows your say is serious.

steps.prompt: Your mother says: "Anything but engineering feels risky. What if it doesn't work out?"

options.text: "It's my life. It's really not your problem."
options.then: She looks stung and leaves the table.

options.text: "Fair worry. Can we look at the options together?"
options.then: She nods slowly. "Together. Okay."

options.text: "Fine. I'll just do engineering, like you want."
options.then: "If that's what you want," she says, unsure.

options.text: "It won't fail. I can promise you that much."
options.then: "You can't promise that," she says.

steps.why: Respecting her worry while keeping your say makes it a real conversation.

scenarios.relearn: Calmly naming a right you hold, while respecting others, is how you claim it.

scenarios.hook: On your first day at college, a senior hands you his bag to carry.

steps.prompt: The senior says: "Freshers have no rights here. Do as you're told."

options.text: "Is that actually written somewhere in the rules?"
options.then: "Unwritten rule," he smirks. "Ask anyone."

options.text: "I'm happy to help out, but I have a right to respect."
options.then: He pauses. "Respect? Relax, it's just fun."

options.text: "Carry your own bag. I'm nobody's servant here."
options.then: His friends hoot. "Ooh, attitude," one says.

options.text: "I guess that's just how college works for freshers."
options.then: "Exactly," he says, dropping the bag at your feet.

steps.why: Calmly naming your right to respect, without insulting him, claims it.

steps.prompt: The senior says: "It's tradition. Everyone did it in our year."

options.text: "So I have to earn respect first?"
options.then: "Exactly," he says. "Now you get it."

options.text: "Traditions that make people feel small aren't fair."
options.then: He shrugs, less sure. "Nobody complained before."

options.text: "Your tradition is pathetic, honestly."
options.then: His smile vanishes. "Watch it, fresher."

options.text: "I'll post about your little tradition tonight."
options.then: "Try it," he says, eyes narrowing.

steps.why: A tradition doesn't cancel anyone's right to respect.

steps.prompt: Later, your friend Nikhil asks: "Should we tell someone about these seniors?"

options.text: "No. Complaining just makes it all worse."
options.then: "Yeah," he says. "Better not."

options.text: "No. Let's just get our own back next year."
options.then: He laughs uneasily. "On the next batch?"

options.text: "Yes. Let's tell a teacher we trust, together."
options.then: "Together," he says. "Okay. Tomorrow."

options.text: "Only if it starts getting really bad."
options.then: "How bad is bad?" he asks.

steps.why: Telling a trusted adult is the safe route, and none of this is your fault.

scenarios.hook: Your chemistry teacher announces that only the girls will skip lab work this term, "for their own safety".

steps.prompt: Your friend Priya is upset, and the class is muttering. What do you do?

options.text: Note what was said, and talk it over with classmates
options.then: Several girls say they want lab practice, and so do two boys.

options.text: Argue with the teacher right there in front of the class
options.then: The teacher gets defensive and says the decision is final.

options.text: Start a mocking meme about the teacher
options.then: The meme spreads, and the teacher digs in harder.

options.text: Decide that's just how things are at this school
options.then: The term starts. The girls copy lab results from the boys' notebooks.

steps.why: Getting the facts and others' views first makes a calm, strong case.

steps.prompt: The next week, lab classes start without the girls. What do you do?

options.text: Raise it calmly with the principal or a senior teacher
options.then: The senior teacher listens and says she'll speak to the principal.

options.text: Ask the teacher to quietly let just you and Priya into the lab
options.then: He agrees for you two. The other girls are still left out.

options.text: Wait and see if he changes his mind by next term
options.then: The term passes, and the girls miss every practical.

options.text: Get parents to flood the school WhatsApp group
options.then: The group fills with angry messages, and the teacher feels attacked.

steps.why: A trusted senior teacher or the principal can fix it for everyone.

steps.prompt: A month later, a classmate says girls don't need labs anyway. What do you say?

options.text: Every student has the same right to learn, labs included
options.then: He shrugs. Later, he admits he'd hate missing labs himself.

options.text: Ignore him, and walk off without a word
options.then: He calls after you that you've got no answer.

options.text: Tell him girls are actually better at science than boys anyway
options.then: He scoffs, and the talk turns into boys versus girls.

options.text: Agree with him, just to avoid an argument
options.then: He takes it as settled and repeats it to others.

steps.why: Equal access to education is a right for every student, whatever their gender.

scenarios.debrief: Unequal access by gender is a rights issue with a school route: the principal or a teacher.
scenarios.relearn: Unequal access by gender: raise it calmly with the principal or a trusted teacher.

scenarios.hook: Your mother's employer hasn't paid her wages for months, and your family can't afford a lawyer.

steps.prompt: Your mother says the courts are only for rich people. What do you say?

options.text: Borrow money from relatives for a private lawyer
options.then: Your mother starts working out loans, and looks more worried.

options.text: You'll find all the answers on YouTube
options.then: You watch three videos that disagree with each other.

options.text: Free legal aid exists, through NALSA 15100
options.then: Your mother looks doubtful. "Free? There must be a catch."

options.text: She's right. There's no point without money
options.then: The topic is dropped, and the unpaid months add up.

steps.why: Free legal aid exists so that cost isn't a barrier to justice.

steps.prompt: A day later, your mother hears from a coworker about free legal help, but doubts it's for families like yours. What do you say?

options.text: You'll call her employer yourself and threaten him tonight
options.then: Your mother panics that she'll lose the job entirely.

options.text: She's probably right, so leave it for now
options.then: She nods. The wages stay unpaid.

options.text: It's meant for people who can't pay. Call together?
options.then: Your mother sighs. "Okay. Let's call tomorrow morning."

options.text: Promise the family will definitely win the case
options.then: Your mother brightens, then asks how you can be so sure.

steps.why: Offering to call together makes the first step easier, without false promises.

steps.prompt: A neighbour hears about it and says free lawyers are useless. What do you say?

options.text: Maybe he's right. You'll drop the idea
options.then: Your mother hears, and starts doubting again.

options.text: Free legal aid is real help, and you'll try it
options.then: The neighbour shrugs and asks for the number, just in case.

options.text: Paid lawyers are all crooks anyway
options.then: The neighbour gets offended, and it turns into a row.

options.text: You can't lose with free help, so it's a sure thing
options.then: The neighbour laughs. "Nobody can promise that."

steps.why: Trying a real route beats rumours, and nobody can honestly promise a result.

scenarios.debrief: Free legal aid via NALSA 15100 means justice isn't only for those who can pay.
scenarios.relearn: Can't afford a lawyer: free legal aid is available via NALSA 15100.

scenarios.hook: On your way home, you see a man being attacked outside a shop. People are filming, not helping.

steps.prompt: He's on the ground, and the attackers haven't stopped. What do you do first?

options.text: Run in and pull the attackers off him
options.then: One attacker shoves you hard into the road.

options.text: Film it for proof before doing anything else
options.then: You get the clip. The man is still on the ground.

options.text: Call 112, and shout for the shopkeeper
options.then: The call connects, and the shopkeeper runs out to help.

options.text: Assume someone else has already called
options.then: Nobody has. The crowd keeps watching.

steps.why: In live danger, 112 comes first. Help arrives sooner, and you stay safe.

steps.prompt: Help arrives, and you realise you're shaking. What do you do next?

options.text: Chase after the attackers to see where they went
options.then: You lose them in the lanes, and you're far from home.

options.text: Post the crowd's videos on your story right away
options.then: The clips spread, with the man's face in full view.

options.text: Call a parent or trusted adult to come and be with you
options.then: Your father arrives in ten minutes and stays while you talk to the police.

options.text: Tell yourself you're fine, since you weren't the one hurt
options.then: You insist you're fine, but that night at home you can't stop shaking.

steps.why: After a shock like that, a trusted adult helps you feel safe and handle what comes next.

steps.prompt: The next day, someone posts a video of the attack, with the man's face clear. What do you do?

options.text: Share it to show people how bad it was
options.then: Your share reaches people who know the man.

options.text: Comment the attackers' names you've heard around
options.then: Someone replies that one name belongs to the wrong person.

options.text: Don't share it, and report the post
options.then: You report it, and two friends do the same.

options.text: Send it privately to a few friends, to talk it over
options.then: One of them forwards it, and by evening it's in another group.

steps.why: Sharing a victim's video spreads harm. Reporting it protects his dignity.

steps.prompt: That evening, a friend says filming is the most useful thing a bystander can do. What do you say?

options.text: Bystanders should always jump in physically
options.then: Your friend looks unsure. "And get hurt too?"

options.text: Agree, because the videos are what really get people justice
options.then: Your friend nods, sure he'd do the same next time.

options.text: It's always wiser never to get involved at all
options.then: Your friend shrugs. "Then who helps?"

options.text: Calling for help comes first. Filming, only after, if safe
options.then: Your friend pauses. "I never thought about the order."

steps.why: Help first, evidence later. That order can save a life.

scenarios.debrief: Live danger routes to help first: emergency 112 and a trusted adult before any 'learn the law' step.
scenarios.relearn: In immediate danger, call emergency 112 and get a trusted adult first.

scenarios.hook: The college debate club turns down your friend Karthik, and a member jokes that it's because of his caste.

steps.prompt: Karthik shrugs it off, but you can tell he's hurt. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him to just try out for a different club instead
options.then: Karthik nods. The club carries on picking the same way.

options.text: Confront the members at their next meeting
options.then: They deny it, and now they know Karthik talked to you.

options.text: Start a pile-on against the club online
options.then: The post spreads, and Karthik is tagged in every comment.

options.text: Ask Karthik how he feels and what he wants to do
options.then: Karthik admits it stung. "I didn't know if it was worth raising."

steps.why: Starting with what Karthik wants keeps him in charge. Being excluded for his caste is never his fault.

steps.prompt: A day later, Karthik says he might raise it but isn't sure how. What do you suggest?

options.text: Going to complain right now, from memory
options.then: The staff member listens, but asks for details Karthik can't recall.

options.text: Getting someone to leak the club's private chats
options.then: A friend sends screenshots, and the club accuses Karthik of spying.

options.text: Writing down what was said, when, and who heard it
options.then: Karthik writes it all out, and a classmate offers to back him up.

options.text: Asking the member to admit it out loud in front of everyone
options.then: The member laughs and says it was only a joke.

steps.why: A clear record helps the right body understand what happened and act.

steps.prompt: The next week, Karthik decides to take it further. Where do you suggest he goes?

options.text: The club president's parents
options.then: They say it's a student matter and hang up.

options.text: The college grievance committee, and you'll go too
options.then: A committee member hears his account and explains the next steps.

options.text: A news channel, for the most pressure
options.then: A reporter calls, and Karthik's name is suddenly everywhere.

options.text: Nowhere official. Just let the club know that he knows
options.then: The club shrugs, and nothing changes.

steps.why: The grievance committee is the body set up to act on discrimination like this.

steps.prompt: A month later, a club member messages Karthik, calling him a troublemaker. What do you suggest?

options.text: Save the message and take it to the grievance committee
options.then: Karthik forwards it, and the committee notes it down with the date.

options.text: Reply with threats of his own
options.then: The member screenshots it and shares it around.

options.text: Apologise to the club to calm things down
options.then: Karthik feels like he's the one who did something wrong.

options.text: Ignore it completely, and tell nobody official about it
options.then: More messages arrive, and nobody official knows.

steps.why: Being pressured for speaking up is something the committee needs to know about.

scenarios.relearn: Caste-based exclusion: document it and take it to the grievance committee or a trusted teacher.

scenarios.hook: A senior at tuition harassed your friend Simran, and she's scared to tell anyone.
scenarios.setup: She whispers it to you at the bus stop.

steps.prompt: Simran pleads: "Please. Can we just forget it happened?"

options.text: "I believe you. You can report it, and I'll come with you."
options.then: Simran hesitates. "You'd come with me? Really?"

options.text: "You have to tell your parents tonight. No excuses."
options.then: Simran pulls back. "I knew I shouldn't have told you."

options.text: "Was it really harassment, though? Maybe he was joking."
options.then: Simran's eyes fill. "Forget I said anything."

options.text: "Okay. If you don't want to do anything, I'll forget it."
options.then: Simran nods, relieved, and stares at the road.

steps.why: Believing her and offering to go together is support, not pressure.

steps.prompt: Simran asks: "What if nobody believes me?"

options.text: "Maybe wait until you have some proof first."
options.then: "Proof?" She looks lost. "I don't have anything."

options.text: "Then we'll post about him so everyone knows."
options.then: "No," she says quickly. "That would make it so much worse."

options.text: "I believe you. A teacher or counsellor will listen too."
options.then: She wipes her eyes. "Ms Fernandes has always been kind."

options.text: "They'll definitely believe you, Simran. I promise you that."
options.then: She looks at you. "You can't know that."

steps.why: It's never her fault. Believing her, and naming someone who'll listen, makes the next step possible.

steps.prompt: Simran says quietly: "If I tell anyone, it can't be today. Maybe next week?"

options.text: "Okay. Meanwhile, block him and act like nothing happened."
options.then: She blocks him. At tuition, he still sits two rows behind her.

options.text: "Okay. Let's pick a day that works, and I'll be with you."
options.then: She nods. "Next Thursday, after school. You'll wait for me?"

options.text: "Sure. And honestly, if it fades, maybe just let it go."
options.then: She smiles weakly, and next week slides into the week after.

options.text: "No. We're going right now, before you change your mind."
options.then: Simran freezes. "I'm not ready," she whispers.

steps.why: A set day respects her pace and still gets her to a trusted adult soon.

steps.prompt: Days later, Simran asks: "If I do tell someone, what if I can't get the words out?"

options.text: "Then maybe wait until you feel braver about it."
options.then: Simran nods, and the weeks slip by.

options.text: "I'll be right there. You can start with one sentence."
options.then: Simran nods. "One sentence. Okay."

options.text: "Then I'll just tell them everything for you."
options.then: Simran looks relieved, then unsure. "But it's my story."

options.text: "You'll be fine. Just try really hard not to cry in front of them."
options.then: Simran's eyes fill. "What if I do?"

steps.why: Staying beside her and keeping it simple helps her speak for herself.

scenarios.relearn: Offer to go with a friend to a trusted adult. Naming their right to report is real support.

scenarios.hook: At your part-time job, the manager, Mr Kohli, keeps touching your arm and calling it a joke.
scenarios.setup: Today you step back, and he laughs.

steps.prompt: Mr Kohli says: "Arre, relax. It's just a joke."

options.text: "My brothers will have something to say about this."
options.then: He laughs. "Your brothers don't work here."

options.text: "Sorry. Maybe I'm being too sensitive about it."
options.then: He smiles. "Good. Don't take everything so seriously."

options.text: "It isn't a joke to me. Please don't touch me."
options.then: He raises his hands. "Okay, okay. So sensitive." He walks off.

options.text: "Do that again and I'll post your name online."
options.then: His smile drops. "Careful. I decide your shifts."

steps.why: Naming it plainly is a boundary, not rudeness. And it is never your fault.

steps.prompt: That night, your mother asks: "Something happened at work, didn't it?"

options.text: "Yes, but it's normal. Every boss jokes around like that."
options.then: She frowns. "What kind of jokes? Tell me exactly."

options.text: "Kind of. But it's probably my fault for being friendly."
options.then: She frowns. "Why would it be your fault? Tell me."

options.text: "Yes. My manager keeps touching me, and it isn't okay."
options.then: She sits beside you. "Thank you for telling me. We'll handle this together."

options.text: "Yes. But promise you won't do anything about it."
options.then: "I can't promise that," she says gently. "Tell me what happened."

steps.why: Telling a trusted adult means you have support. You don't have to handle it alone.

steps.prompt: Later, once she's heard everything, your mother asks: "What would you like to do about it?"

options.text: "Let's post his name in the neighbourhood group."
options.then: She shakes her head. "That could come back on you. Is there a proper way?"

options.text: "Write it all down and take it to the Internal Committee."
options.then: She nods. "I'll come with you. Let's write it down tonight."

options.text: "Ask the owner to have a quiet word with him, nothing written."
options.then: She hesitates. "And if a quiet word doesn't stop him?"

options.text: "Let's go and shout at him in the shop tomorrow."
options.then: "That could turn ugly," she says. "And it puts you in the middle."

steps.why: The Internal Committee is the route for this, and a written record helps it act.

steps.prompt: A few days later, your coworker Meena says: "He does that to me too. I thought it was normal."

options.text: "It's normal here, I guess. Just ignore it."
options.then: Meena shrugs. "I suppose that's how it is."

options.text: "That's not normal or your fault. Let's go to the committee."
options.then: Meena hesitates, then nods. "Okay. Together."

options.text: "Let's both quit and post about him everywhere."
options.then: Meena looks scared. "I really need this job."

options.text: "Keep it to yourself for now. I'll handle my own complaint first."
options.then: Meena nods, and keeps her own story quiet.

steps.why: Telling her it's not her fault, and offering company, helps her use the route too.

scenarios.relearn: Name the harassment and take it to the Internal Committee. You don't have to laugh it off.

scenarios.hook: Your aunt is arranging a wedding for your 16-year-old cousin Lakshmi.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "This is family business. Stay out of it."

options.text: "This is a crime, and I'll get you all arrested."
options.then: The table goes silent. Your aunt glares at you.

options.text: "I care about her. She's under 18 and wants to finish school."
options.then: He sighs. "You young people think it's all so simple."

options.text: "You're right, Uncle. It's not my place to say."
options.then: He nods, satisfied, and goes back to his plate.

options.text: "Fine. But at least let her choose the boy herself, Uncle."
options.then: He shrugs. "We'll see. The date is already fixed."

steps.why: Calmly naming her age and her wish to study keeps the focus on Lakshmi, not a fight.

steps.prompt: Later, Lakshmi finds you and whispers: "Please don't make it worse for me."

scenarios.hook: Someone you chatted with online is now threatening to leak your chats.
scenarios.setup: The message pops up late at night.

steps.prompt: They write: "Pay up or everyone sees these."

options.text: "Why are you doing this? I thought we were friends."
options.then: "Friends pay," they reply. "Tonight."

options.text: "I won't pay. I'm saving this and reporting it."
options.then: They send an angry emoji and a countdown, then go quiet.

options.text: "I'll find out who you are and get you beaten up."
options.then: "Big talk," they write, and the threats get nastier.

options.text: "You're bluffing. Go ahead and post them, then."
options.then: "Don't test me," comes the reply, with a screenshot of your chat.

steps.why: A short refusal, then saving everything, takes away their power. It's not your fault.

steps.prompt: Your older sister Divya knocks and asks: "Why are you still up? You look scared."

options.text: "Promise you'll never, ever tell Mum and Papa."
options.then: Divya hesitates. "I can't promise that if you're in trouble."

options.text: "Someone's threatening me online. Can I show you?"
options.then: Divya sits beside you. "Show me. You did nothing wrong."

options.text: "I messed up really badly, Didi. It's all my own fault."
options.then: "What happened?" she asks, worried. "Whatever it is, tell me."

options.text: "They're just bluffing. These things are never real."
options.then: Divya looks at the screen. "It looks real to me. Show me."

steps.why: Telling someone you trust means you're no longer facing the threat alone.

steps.prompt: Divya sees the threat on your screen and asks: "Okay. What do we do now?"

options.text: "Delete everything, so there's nothing left to leak."

options.text: "You message them from your own phone and scare them off."
options.then: Divya frowns. "That might just make them angrier."

options.text: "Let's just report the account in the app and sleep."
options.then: Divya taps report. "Done. But they could just make a new account."

options.text: "Report it at cybercrime.gov.in or 1930, and tell Mum."
options.then: Divya nods. "Let's wake her and do it together."

steps.why: The portal and a trusted adult are the real route. You never have to pay.

options.text: "Don't pay. Save the threats, tell an adult, and report it."

options.text: "Threaten them right back. That's what I'd do."
options.then: Kunal types a threat, and the reply comes with a deadline.

scenarios.hook: You're 17, and the school office has charged your exam fee twice.
scenarios.setup: The clerk barely looks up from his desk.

steps.prompt: The clerk says: "You're a minor. You can't complain about anything."

options.text: "Oh. Okay, I'll just leave it, then."
options.then: He nods and calls the next student.

options.text: "I can still raise it, and a parent can come with me."
options.then: He shrugs. "Then bring a parent. Next."

options.text: "That's illegal. I'm going to sue this school."
options.then: He laughs. "Go ahead. Next."

options.text: "Can't you make an exception for me, sir, just this once?"
options.then: "Rules are rules," he says, and turns away.

steps.prompt: At home, your father asks: "Is it worth fighting the school over this?"

options.text: "I'll post online about the school cheating us out of fees."
options.then: "Careful," he says. "You still have to study there."

options.text: "Can you just go alone and shout at them for me?"
options.then: He frowns. "Shouting won't help. What's the actual problem?"

options.text: "It's our money, and we can ask. Will you come with me?"
options.then: He considers it. "All right. Friday, before work."

options.text: "No, forget it. It's not worth the trouble."
options.then: He nods, then pauses. "Actually, it's our money. Let's at least ask on Friday."

steps.why: Asking an adult to come with you turns a brush-off into a proper request.

steps.prompt: Back at the office, the clerk says: "Write to the principal. We can't refund it here."

options.text: "Then we'll take this straight to the local newspapers instead."
options.then: The clerk rolls his eyes. "As you like."

options.text: "Forget it, then. It's too much trouble."
options.then: The clerk shrugs and goes back to his screen.

options.text: "Can't you just refund it in cash, off the record?"
options.then: "No," he says flatly. "Nothing off the record here."

options.text: "We'll write today, with receipts, and ask for a reply."
options.then: The clerk slides over a form. "Attach the receipts there."

steps.why: A written request with receipts follows the route and gives the school a clear record.

steps.prompt: A week later, your father says: "The school still hasn't refunded it. What now?"

options.text: "Let's give up. Schools always win in the end."
options.then: He sighs. "Maybe you're right."

options.text: "Let's tell every parent to stop paying fees."
options.then: "That could hurt a lot of families," he says.

options.text: "I'll find a lawyer online who promises us a quick refund."
options.then: "Promises cost money," he says. "Let's be careful."

options.text: "Let's ask free legal aid, NALSA 15100, what we can do."
options.then: He writes down the number. "I'll call in my lunch break."

steps.why: Free legal aid can point you to the route, so age or money isn't a barrier.

scenarios.relearn: Being under 18 doesn't end your routes; a trusted adult and free legal aid can help.

options.text: "You don't deserve this. Let's tell a teacher together."

options.text: "I'll go and sort out the guy who started all this, right now."

options.text: "Maybe just slip the teacher an anonymous note."
